articles.title: What is next for Israel?
articles.summary: The message of the vote is that the violent Israeli policies within occupied territory and the region will continue.
articles.preview: The message of the Israeli vote is that the violent Israeli policies within occupied territory and the region will continue. There are two ways to read the results of the Israeli elections. One way would be to see them as a defeat for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. From holding a solid majority in the 120-member Knesset, the Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers, by contrast, hold 67 seats.
articles.body:
The message of the Israeli vote is that the violent Israeli policies within occupied territory and the region will continue.

There are two ways to read the results of the Israeli elections. One way would be to see them as a defeat for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. From holding a solid majority in the 120-member Knesset, the Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers, by contrast, hold 67 seats.

Had Israel been a democracy, we would have seen scenes of celebration similar to the ones we saw this year in Hungary, Brazil and Serbia, where political forces with undemocratic tendencies were defeated. But Israel is not a democracy, and Netanyahu was not necessarily defeated.

The second, more relevant way of reading the results of the Israeli election would necessitate accepting the apartheid nature of Israel and seeing the electoral arithmetic through that prism. In this case, Netanyahu won because he secured 53 seats in the Knesset – five more than the anti-Netanyahu Jewish bloc.

To form a government, a bloc needs to have the support of at least 61 members of the Knesset. The only way Netanyahu can do it is by enticing parties or lawmakers from the anti-Netanyahu bloc to join his bloc, as he has succeeded in doing many times in the past. Working with Palestinian parties, which secured 19 seats, is out of the question for him.

The obvious path for government formation for the anti-Netanyahu bloc would be to form a coalition – one that would include the two Palestinian parties. But to do so would mean to challenge Israeli apartheid. The main leaders of the Jewish anti-Netanyahu bloc, including Gadi Eisenkot, have promised not to do so under any circumstances.

There is another option: seeking the support of the religious Orthodox parties, which have so far been part of the Netanyahu bloc. To secure their backing, the anti-Netanyahu bloc would have to promise to exempt religious Orthodox youth from military service and guarantee funding for their learning centres.

However, Eisenkot’s main election promise was forcing young Haredi Jews into the army. So this is not a very likely scenario, but in politics, never say never.

There is also the option of a “unity government” led by some sort of rotation between the leading figures of the anti-Netanyahu bloc and Netanyahu. The problem here is that, according to a law passed a few years ago, as long as Netanyahu is still a defendant in an ongoing trial, he cannot serve as a minister; his coalition made sure that the legislation ridiculously would not apply to a prime minister.

Given that Netanyahu’s corruption trial is destined to go on for a very long time, the rotation would make it impossible for Netanyahu to be part of a government under Eisenkot as prime minister. That means he would demand to hold the rotating premiership first and leave open the option to collapse the government once his rotation is over.

Netanyahu has already done that before. In 2020, without any hesitation, he broke a rotation agreement with Benny Gantz, who had naively believed that after two years he would be the prime minister. This resulted in new elections, which Netanyahu won.

Finally, a very possible scenario is that neither of the two blocs would be able to form a government, which would mean new elections in six months. Netanyahu and his government would remain in office until the new polls, albeit with more limited authority.

This would give them the opportunity to reignite a war with Iran and Hezbollah and continue with their violent policies in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank in an attempt to attract more public support and win the elections.

This is the preferred option for Netanyahu because his relative defeat in the October 27 elections had a lot to do with the unprecedented galvanisation among the Palestinian voters in Israel and the more liberal Jewish Israelis living abroad who came back home in huge numbers to vote.

These possible scenarios tell only part of the story and are not enough to fully understand what the election results mean for Israel, the Palestinians and the region. Here are the more important conclusions one should draw from the results:

The first pertains to the future of the Palestinian citizens of Israel. They still could turn out to vote in large numbers if new elections are held soon. But if they are once more ignored and sidelined by the other political parties, they will never try it again.

In this case, it would be difficult for the leadership of this community to continue to delay a strategic decision: choosing which political space Palestinian citizens of Israel belong to – the Israeli or the Palestinian one?

Until today, they have given a chance to the Israeli political system despite its racism, apartheid tendencies and criminal policies towards Palestinians. Palestinian parties recommended Eisenkot for the premiership to President Isaac Herzog, who has now tasked him with forming a government.

If I can venture a prediction – and it is only a prediction – the anti-Netanyahu bloc would not engage meaningfully with the Palestinian parties. Its message, therefore, will be that the Palestinians of Israel are not legitimate players in the Israeli political field.

If I am wrong, this would be an incredible and transformative moment in the history of both Israel and Palestine, but there seems to be very little hope for such a development.

There are other lessons we can learn from where we are now with the knowledge that this is a very volatile moment in the history of Israel.

The first and most important one is that whoever forms the next government of Israel will continue the incremental genocide in Gaza, the intensified ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and the aggressive policies towards the region. These policies as before can only be stopped or tamed by the region and the international community sending a clear message to Israel that there will be a price tag attached to such policies.

The second lesson is that the Israeli Jewish society is as deeply divided as ever, to the point that it is impossible for it to maintain a stable political system, a thriving economy and a positive strategy towards the region and the world.

The third lesson is that Israel’s international isolation will increase as a result of this trajectory, including the continued dissociation from Zionism among young Jews around the world, including in the United States.

Finally and most importantly, this can have an impact on the global discussion about Zionism. The move by the Green Party in Britain to define Zionism as racism – despite being currently an exception and widely condemned – will gain validity with time.

These elections and future developments are making clear that Zionism in the current Israeli politics means the exclusion of Palestinian citizens of Israel from politics – first by ignoring them and quite possibly in the future by denying them the right to vote

Moreover, many in the international community will associate the term Zionism with a consensual Israeli policy of genocide, ethnic cleansing and apartheid.

The outlook in the short term is worrying. The overall message from the Israeli elections is that the future policies of the state will continue to threaten the lives of the Palestinians in occupied territory, Palestinian citizens of Israel, and the people of southern Lebanon and Syria. There will be more instability in the region.

In the long run, however, as bad as it is, the fundamental cracks in the Zionist project will widen, which might lead to its demise. One can only hope this will also lead to the beginning of a political reality that would benefit everyone who lives in historical Palestine and the region.

A version of this oped was first published by Al Jazeera Arabic.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: How Israel’s separation wall compares with the Berlin Wall
articles.summary: How Israel's wall, checkpoints and permits divide Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and cut farmers off from land.
articles.preview: How Israel’s wall, checkpoints and permits divide Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and cut farmers off from land. articles.body:
How Israel’s wall, checkpoints and permits divide Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and cut farmers off from land.

In the occupied West Bank, a barrier of concrete and fencing cuts Palestinians off from their land, their families and nearby towns.

Israel began building its separation wall in 2002. Planned to stretch 712km (442 miles), it runs deep inside Palestinian territory rather than along the boundary with Israel. In 2004, the International Court of Justice ruled it illegal.

Today’s date carries extra weight. Thirty-seven years ago on November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

Built by East Germany in 1961 to stop its citizens fleeing to the West, it encircled West Berlin for 155km (96 miles), dividing the city and its people for 28 years.

Since 2003, Palestinians have marked the same date as an international day of action against Israel’s wall, which is more than four times as long and still being built. In urban areas, its concrete rises to about 9 metres (30ft), more than twice the height of Berlin’s.

But the wall is more than a physical structure. It operates alongside a wider network of checkpoints, roadblocks, gates and permits that restricts Palestinian movement across the occupied territory.

Where does the wall run?

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 456km (283 miles), or 64 percent, of the planned route had been built by April.

About 85 percent of it runs inside the West Bank rather than along the Green Line, the 1949 armistice line separating Israel from the West Bank. That route determines which communities, roads and farmland are cut off from their surroundings.

In some urban areas, the barrier is a concrete wall. Elsewhere, it is made up of fences, patrol roads, ditches and other security infrastructure.

For Palestinians, the comparison with Berlin carries a message. “It doesn’t matter how high the barriers will be, they will fall,” a Palestinian activist in Bir Nabala told Al Jazeera. “Like the Berlin Wall fell, the Palestinian wall will fall.”

How many people are cut off from their land?

The wall’s impact reaches far beyond the structure itself. Its route cuts Palestinian communities off from neighbouring towns, workplaces and farmland, disrupting livelihoods and everyday life.

More than 14,000 Palestinians live between the wall and the Green Line in an area known as the Seam Zone. To reach basic services, markets and relatives on the other side, they must pass through checkpoints.

Farmers are among the hardest hit. According to OCHA, about 150 Palestinian communities have land in this area. Reaching it depends on permits, prior coordination with Israeli authorities and access through designated agricultural gates.

There are about 62 such gates along the wall, and most stay closed for much of the year. During the 2025 olive harvest, 74 percent opened only on a limited number of days.

In Qalqiliya, the wall wraps around much of the city, cutting it off from nearby Palestinian communities and the land around it. Journeys to neighbouring towns that were once short can now mean passing through checkpoints or taking long detours.

The wall restricts more than movement. It reshapes how communities relate to their land and places that are part of their everyday lives.

Israel’s wider system of control

The wall is only one part of a much wider network restricting Palestinian movement across the West Bank.

As of December, OCHA documented 925 checkpoints, road gates, earth mounds and other obstacles across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. They restrict the movement of about 3.4 million Palestinians, often forcing long detours to reach work, school, hospitals and other services.

The network includes 89 permanently staffed checkpoints, 218 partial checkpoints, 232 road gates, 167 earth mounds, 114 linear closures and 105 roadblocks.

Checkpoints and road gates now make up nearly 60 percent of these obstacles, up from 15 percent two decades ago when temporary blockages, such as earth mounds and roadblocks, were far more common.

Crossing the wall itself requires permits. Of its 13 checkpoints, only three can be used by Palestinians with West Bank IDs and Israeli-issued permits to enter East Jerusalem and Israel. OCHA said these permits are hard to get and many have been revoked or suspended since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

The wall stretches for hundreds of kilometres, but its impact cannot be measured by distance alone. It is measured in the farmland farmers struggle to reach, the communities cut off from nearby towns and the checkpoints between people and the places they need to go.

WELLINGTON – New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is on course to hang on to power as the head of a coalition government with a razor-thin majority following Saturday’s election, but his National Party could lose control of key government ministries to right-wing partners.

Center-right National and the main opposition Labour Party both polled below 30% for the first time ever, losing votes to minor parties on the left, right and center — a trend that analysts said mirrored a global shift away from the political establishment.

Preliminary New Zealand Electoral Commission data shows Luxon’s three-party coalition could govern with a majority of just two seats. But that margin may disappear once overseas and other special votes — which make up a seventh of the total and typically skew left — are included during the final count on Nov. 27.

articles.body:
Fixing Britain’s youth jobs crisis will require ministers to drastically increase investment in employment support while avoiding arbitrary cuts to benefits, the head of the trade union movement has said.

Before an important official report expected next week, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said the government had a “once in a generation chance” to secure young people’s futures.

In an interview with the Guardian before the highly anticipated Milburn review into young people and work, he said the costs of increasing job support, education and training would be outweighed by economic gains that would help to ease the pressure on the welfare state.

“There is no solution that is cost-free,” he said. “The government is going to have to be prepared to invest in securing the future of those young people, but also to invest to secure what is the future of our economy.

“This is where the government is going to have to be clear. Of course as a country it’s right to invest in our physical infrastructure, but also we have to invest in social infrastructure too.”

Ministers are braced for the report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour health secretary, to recommend welfare cuts to fund job support for almost a million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).

The report was delayed until after the budget amid fears that the call for welfare cuts would sit uneasily alongside the tax and spending plans of the chancellor, John Healey.

Andy Burnham has said the surge in young people who are Neet is an “economic catastrophe and a moral failure” and that tougher benefits rules and more help for young people will form part of his government’s response to the Milburn report.

The prime minister has been at pains to take a cautious approach to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion, which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn on planned disability benefit cuts within a year of coming to power.

Calling on Burnham to focus on delivering a step change in employment support, Nowak said increased investment would help to bring down the benefits bill by getting more young people into work.

“We can’t afford to not do this stuff, as the benefits bill will go up if young people are not supported,” he said.

“I don’t think this government is going to repeat the mistake of the previous attempt at benefit reform, where you make arbitrary cuts, [and] where you have an impact on some of the most vulnerable people without thinking about how you support people into work.”

There is rising concern over youth worklessness. Most Britons now see the youth jobs crisis as one of the biggest problems facing the country – ranking it second only to the cost of living and above NHS waiting lists, housing, crime and immigration, according to polling by the research company Focaldata for the Jobs Foundation.

The employment charity, co-founded by the Conservative peer Matthew Elliott, is behind a national campaign to tackle worklessness that launches on Monday. It includes a pledge, backed by a group of leading employers – including Amazon, Pret a Manger, NatWest, Marks & Spencer and Shell – that have committed to support young people who have been overlooked for work.

A government spokesperson said: “We are determined to turn the tide on youth unemployment which has been years in the making.

“We have already pledged £2.5bn in youth employment support, which will deliver almost 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn, while engaging with business including some of Britain’s biggest retail and hospitality brands to create up to 200,000 jobs for young people.

“Further reform will follow the Milburn review, which will be published in the autumn.”

articles.title: ‘Tents don’t protect us’: Rains flood displaced Palestinians in Gaza
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians are vulnerable to flooding as Israel continues to block entry of mobile homes.
articles.preview: Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians are vulnerable to flooding as Israel continues to block the entry of mobile homes into Gaza. Az-Zawayda, Gaza Strip – On Saturday night, water began rushing into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent in central Gaza’s az-Zawayda area, waking him and his family as heavy rain swept across Gaza. Soon the tent’s floor was flooded, soaking mattresses, carpets, blankets and spoiling what little food the family had managed to keep.
articles.body:
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians are vulnerable to flooding as Israel continues to block the entry of mobile homes into Gaza.

Az-Zawayda, Gaza Strip – On Saturday night, water began rushing into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent in central Gaza’s az-Zawayda area, waking him and his family as heavy rain swept across Gaza. Soon the tent’s floor was flooded, soaking mattresses, carpets, blankets and spoiling what little food the family had managed to keep.

“Everyone woke up and stayed awake, asking their neighbours about the extent of damage and inquiring about children,” Jaber, who is in his 70s, told Al Jazeera.

He described the area outside the displacement camp, where thousands of Palestinians have taken refuge, as a swimming pool.

More than 70,000 tents have been flooded since heavy rains began late on Friday, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians are sheltering in locations considered “highly vulnerable” to more flooding.

More than a year after the so-called “ceasefire” deal was signed between Israel and Hamas, Israel has continued to flout the terms of the agreement, blocking the entry of goods into Gaza, including 60,000 mobile homes and 200,000 tents.

Only 20,000 tents have been allowed in, and mobile homes have remained parked on the Egyptian side of the border, many of them for more than two years.

Fourth winter in tents

This is the fourth winter for Jaber and his family living in a tent house in the az-Zawayda area. Originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, Jaber has been displaced several times, like most Palestinians since Israel launched its genocidal war on October 7, 2023.

More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been displaced, many of them multiple times, by the war that has attracted global condemnation.

Jaber says his camp was flooded three or four times last winter, forcing many families to leave. Around 40 tents still remain there, but the latest flooding has left them in even worse condition.

“All the tents are now damaged, torn and covered in mud,” Jaber told Al Jazeera.

“We urgently need tents, tarpaulins, plastic sheets, mattresses, blankets and carpets to protect us from the difficult days ahead.

“We keep hearing about tents and tarpaulins being distributed, but we have received nothing.

“We had hoped the mobile homes and temporary housing units promised under the ceasefire deal would allow us to rest and return to a life of safety and peace. But it was all just words in the air. We have seen nothing.”

Promised shelter, unmet needs

Jaber’s experience reflects the wider shelter crisis facing displaced Palestinians across Gaza. Despite the “ceasefire” agreement, which included provisions for temporary housing units, tents and heavy machinery to clear rubble, large numbers of families remain in makeshift shelters exposed to winter weather.

Under the first phase of the agreement, along with temporary housing units and tents, heavy equipment was also supposed to be allowed in to remove rubble and help restore damaged infrastructure.

But the arrival of mobile homes and heavy machinery has been delayed as Israel has found excuses to restrict their entry into the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Trucks carrying mobile homes and equipment have reportedly been waiting on the Egyptian side of the border while Palestinians live in misery in dilapidated tent camps.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Gaza requires approximately 121,000 tents and 561,000 tarpaulins, while available stocks remain far below what is needed.

For Om Hani Hamouda, a displaced woman from Beit Lahiya now sheltering in al-Zawayda, replacing her worn-out tent with a caravan has become a dream.

“We did not expect that the first rainfall would leave us in this condition,” she told Al Jazeera. “These tents do not protect us from the cold, storms or rain. Whenever winter comes, everyone holds their breath.”

Hamouda had hoped the ceasefire agreement would allow her family to return to northern Gaza or at least receive a caravan or building materials to secure better shelter. But she said there had been no sign of progress.

“We are asking for a dignified life. We want these tents to be replaced with caravans. Even a simple caravan would be better,” she told Al Jazeera.

Hamouda’s family has been displaced around 15 times during the war. She spent more than 15 years living and working in the United Arab Emirates before returning to Gaza nearly two years before the war began.

“My children cry because they miss the life we had there,” she said. “Life here is so difficult. There is no life in any sense.”

Families left exposed to the rain

Ramy Abdu, chairman of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, told Al Jazeera that large quantities of tents, caravans, prefabricated housing units and shelter equipment remain stranded at Gaza’s borders because of Israeli restrictions.

He said that while more than 1.5 million displaced Palestinians were facing another winter in worn-out tents, even people living in houses and apartments remained exposed to the elements because of the extensive damage to homes and infrastructure.

“Today, we cannot even say that those living in houses and apartments are safe from extreme weather because, with around 85 percent of homes destroyed or damaged, every family is exposed to some degree of harsh weather conditions,” Abdu said, adding that Israel continues to reject shipments containing timber and emergency shelter kits, depriving families of the ability to repair homes that could otherwise accommodate them.

Abdu said Israel, as the occupying power, was legally obligated under the Fourth Geneva Convention to ensure essential supplies reached civilians and to facilitate humanitarian relief.

Jihad Dawwas, 51, says he felt helpless as he could not do anything as his children had nowhere dry to sleep amid the rains.

Water poured into the tents at the displacement camp where he is sheltering, while strong winds blew away many of the surrounding tents. His children ended up sleeping while standing, he said, after rainwater soaked their mattresses and the plastic sheets covering their shelter.

“They slept standing up. By morning, some of my children had become ill because of the cold and the storm,” he told Al Jazeera.

Dawwas, who was displaced from northern Gaza, is sheltering with seven of his own children and three orphaned children of his brother. He said he had bought the family’s tent with his own money and had received no tent from any charity or aid initiative.

“A tent cannot replace a home, not even by one percent,” he said. “We are living in what is left of our lives.”

He said he had seen no caravans or temporary housing units arrive to help displaced families, despite the expectations raised by the ceasefire agreement.

“Our lives are a daily hell. We are completely forgotten. There is no fair distribution of aid, and no one is really asking about us,” Dawwas said.

He questioned why even basic shelter supplies had become so difficult to obtain.

“Do tents and tarpaulins really need all this pressure and effort just to become something we can ask for?” he asked. “They should provide us with tents and tarpaulins, and give us at least a dignified life.”

articles.body:
Victorian Labor MPs are both sceptical and seriously concerned about a new poll ahead of the state election showing the party trailing third behind One Nation, with its primary vote at an all-time low of just 18%.

The DemosAU/PremierNational, first published by the Herald Sun on Monday, showed Labor’s primary vote share has crashed seven points to 18%, putting it in third place behind the Coalition’s 33% and One Nation’s 21%. At the same time, the Greens improved their primary vote to 17%, an increase of three points since September.

It means the Coalition now leads Labor on a two-party preferred basis 56-44, compared with 52-48 in September.

George Hasanakos, DemosAU’s head of research, said if the poll were replicated on election night then many contests across the state would be between the Liberals or Nationals and One Nation, which would then result in a “clear Coalition majority”.

“If that happens, One Nation has to poll really, really well to have a chance of winning, because Labor and Greens preferences will flow to the Liberals,” he said.

On election night, the Victorian Electoral Commission plans to conduct a two-candidate-preferred count, or 2CP, between the two candidates it expects to finish with the most support after preferences are distributed. The commission is selecting the indicative 2CP for each seat based on polling, analysis of preference flows and results from previous elections. It will not publish the indicative 2CPs before election day to avoid influencing voter behaviour.

Hasanakos added that he “double, triple, quadruple checked” the result of the “extraordinary” poll, which had 1,562 respondents, an effective sample of 818 and a margin of error of 3.4%.

“We went to the trouble of a bigger sample here, and I stand by it,” he said.

Ben Carroll repeatedly refused to say whether he was worried about the poll at a press conference in South Melbourne on Monday morning.

“What I’m focused on every day is fighting for working people and making sure that every Victorian that goes into the ballot on November 28 knows that under my government you have a government on your side that will fight for you,” he told reporters.

“The alternative is a Liberal-One Nation government that will fight against you – they’re going to shrink the economy, cause a recession and make life difficult for every single Victorian.”

But the result has sparked serious concerns among the Labor caucus, even though some MPs are sceptical about the 18% figure. Inside Labor’s campaign headquarters, they are treating the result as an “outlier” and point to other public polls that have their primary vote in the 20s.

Several Labor MPs, unauthorised to speak publicly, have told Guardian Australia there are many in the caucus questioning their party’s strategy.

This includes a focus in recent days on crime – an issue that is typically a Coalition strength. On Sunday, Carroll announced a $204m plan to enable judges to sentence low- and mid-level youth offenders to a new rehabilitation detention program, while on Monday he announced $70m to recruit 200 more police reservists to reopen stations and build and upgrade more stations.

“Caucus is really angry and deflated, because this is all happening because of him,” one MP said.

“Even if it’s higher than 18, and we get back into something with a two in front of it, the experiment has been an epic fail, the campaign is in freefall, and it’s about to get a whole lot worse.”

Another MP said the focus on crime was “diabolically stupid strategy” as the government had years to tackle community concern around rising rates.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Monday said her party had a focus on “getting tough on crime”, including by introducing Aidan’s Law to toughen sentencing for attacks on people who step in to protect others.

Carroll immediately matched the commitment to introduce the proposed law, named after 22-year-old Aidan Becker, who was fatally stabbed at Mernda station after stepping in to protect a 14-year-old during an alleged violent robbery.

It comes as Pauline Hanson rejected reports by the Age and 60 Minutes on Sunday that her former national campaign director Sean Black continues to secretly work for One Nation in Victoria.

Black in 2018 was jailed for rape and subsequently lost his appeal against the conviction but was then rehired by One Nation in 2020 as a campaign director after serving his time. Hanson sacked him after political pressure earlier this year.

She told the Australian Financial Review on Monday “the day that I sacked him [Sean Black] that was the day he finished up”.

articles.title: I piani di Bukele per Haiti
articles.summary: Il presidente del Salvador ha mandato più di duemila soldati nel paese caraibico per salvare quattro connazionali scomparsi. Una missione che solleva molte preoccupazioni
articles.preview: Dopo il presunto rapimento il 18 ottobre di quattro tecnici dell’aviazione salvadoregni in una zona della capitale haitiana Port-au-Prince controllata dalle bande criminali, alla fine del mese il presidente populista del Salvador Nayib Bukele ha inviato nel paese caraibico 2.500 soldati, “trasformando la missione di salvataggio in un’operazione militare su vasta scala”, scrive il sito indipendente El Faro.
articles.body:
Dopo il presunto rapimento il 18 ottobre di quattro tecnici dell’aviazione salvadoregni in una zona della capitale haitiana Port-au-Prince controllata dalle bande criminali, alla fine del mese il presidente populista del Salvador Nayib Bukele ha inviato nel paese caraibico 2.500 soldati, “trasformando la missione di salvataggio in un’operazione militare su vasta scala”, scrive il sito indipendente El Faro. I quattro salvadoregni facevano parte della Gang suppression force (Gsf), una forza internazionale di polizia approvata a giugno dalle Nazioni Unite e sostenuta da Washington per combattere la violenza delle bande criminali.

“Non si tratta di un’operazione contro il popolo haitiano, né di un’invasione di Haiti. Non siamo una grande potenza. Non abbiamo alcun interesse a dominare il popolo haitiano, né ad appropriarci delle ricchezze di Haiti. Siamo un paese modesto e in via di sviluppo. Tutto ciò che vogliamo è che i nostri quattro tecnici aeronautici tornino a casa. E daremo una lezione alle bande criminali, quelle bande che stanno facendo soffrire il popolo haitiano, che uccidono persone amate dalla nazione, che impediscono loro di vivere una vita normale e libera dalla paura”, ha scritto Bukele su X il 4 novembre.

Durante una conferenza stampa in occasione della visita della presidente peruviana Keiko Fujimori, il presidente salvadoregno ha aggiunto che “come abbiamo sconfitto le bande criminali nel Salvador, possiamo farlo anche ad Haiti, sta agli haitiani decidere se lasciarci agire o meno”.

Il 30 ottobre un articolo di Axios ha rivelato che l’invio dei soldati nel paese caraibico ha ricevuto l’appoggio degli Stati Uniti, oltre al supporto logistico della Repubblica Dominicana e della Colombia. Tuttavia Bukele ha sottolineato che il 90 per cento dei costi dell’operazione è a carico del Salvador.

Scontri a fuoco

Ad Haiti l’accoglienza è stata mista. Widlore Mérancourt, un giornalista haitiano dell’AyiboPost e collaboratore regolare del Washington Post, ha detto che alcuni cittadini sono talmente stanchi degli abusi delle bande criminali e dell’assenza dello stato che ammirano i metodi repressivi usati da Bukele per ridurre la violenza nel suo paese e sono favorevoli al suo intervento per cambiare la situazione sull’isola; ma c’è anche chi si chiede in che modo le truppe del leader salvadoregno s’inseriranno nell’attuale struttura di sicurezza di Haiti.

“Alcuni segnali fanno pensare che Bukele voglia che il suo personale operi autonomamente rispetto alla Gsf. E questo ha suscitato preoccupazione tra i difensori dei diritti umani e le organizzazioni della società civile per quanto riguarda le regole di ingaggio, la responsabilità, il rischio di un’escalation di violenza e le possibili vittime civili in territori che le forze straniere, appena arrivate, conoscono a malapena”, ha spiegato Mérancourt al Faro.

In effetti un aumento della violenza si è già registrato. Il 28 ottobre Medici senza frontiere (Msf) ha reso noto che in alcuni quartieri della capitale ci sono stati scontri a fuoco con diversi feriti, tra cui donne e bambini. Dopo il 18 ottobre, quando sono scomparsi i quattro funzionari salvadoregni, negli ospedali gestiti da Msf a Tabarre e a Cité Soleil sono arrivati pazienti con ferite da armi da fuoco e ustioni per le esplosioni di droni. Inoltre, alcuni feriti in gravi condizioni hanno impiegato ore per raggiungere gli ospedali, perché molte strade e diversi ponti erano stati bloccati dalle bande.

Secondo il quotidiano Miami Herald, “questo dispiegamento militare, unito al silenzio dei funzionari haitiani, suscita preoccupazioni sulla portata della missione, sulla sua legittimità giuridica, sulle sue implicazioni per la sicurezza di Haiti e sulla risposta internazionale alla crisi della sicurezza nel paese. Inoltre solleva dubbi sulla sovranità di Haiti, visto che Bukele ha mandato le truppe senza aver prima raggiunto un accordo con le autorità haitiane”.

Le Nazioni Unite stanno prendendo le distanze dal dispiegamento di forza senza precedenti voluto da Bukele, confermando che la maggioranza delle truppe della nazione centroamericana sta operando al di fuori della Gsf autorizzata dal Consiglio di sicurezza e al di là del mandato e delle linee guida dell’ufficio di supporto delle Nazioni Unite. A questo si aggiunge il problema che le truppe fanno capo a un comandante salvadoregno a Port-au-Prince invece che al generale di divisione mongolo responsabile della missione multinazionale.

Questo articolo è tratto dalla newsletter Sudamericana.

articles.body:
The blaze broke out in a building in Shanxi province's Taiyuan city around 5pm on Sunday (Nov 8)

BEIJING: A fire that broke out in an apartment building in northern China killed at least 14 people, state media said on Monday (Nov 9), raising the death toll from the previous night.

Deadly fires are relatively common in China due to lax building codes and an often slipshod approach to workplace safety.

The blaze occurred in a building in Shanxi province's Taiyuan city around 5pm on Sunday, the official Xinhua news agency said that evening.

"A total of 38 people were sent to hospitals for treatment, among whom five have died," Xinhua reported, raising the death toll to 14 on Monday morning.

The flames were extinguished on Sunday, with search and rescue efforts completed, it said.

The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

China launched a campaign against fire hazards in high-rise buildings last November, after a huge blaze engulfed several tower blocks in Hong Kong, killing 168 people.

A month later, a fire at a residential building in southern China's Guangdong province killed 12 people.

And in July, a fire that engulfed a shoe factory in eastern China killed at least 28 people.

articles.title: How a digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president
articles.summary: Until March 2025, impeached Paraguayan President Santiago Pena had been a business partner of the group that owns Ueno Bank.
articles.preview: ASUNCION, PARAGUAY – For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, Ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time. But over just five days last week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.
articles.body:
ASUNCION, PARAGUAY – For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, Ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time.

But over just five days last week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.

On Friday evening, Paraguayan President Santiago Pena was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement.

articles.title: I libri scelti da Internazionale
articles.summary: Da “Non correte! Andate piano!” di Roman Polanski a Grazie di Pablo Katchadjian. Le recensioni della stampa straniera
articles.preview: Il regista Roman Polanski aveva già raccontato la sua infanzia durante la guerra in un’autobiografia: il muro che nel 1941 vede sorgere intorno al ghetto di Cracovia, i genitori deportati, la madre morta ad Auschwitz, il rifugio presso contadini polacchi. In “Non correte! Andate piano!” torna su quel passato. Per quanto gravi siano i fatti di violenza sessuale per i quali ha riportato condanne o è stato accusato, sarebbe un peccato non leggere il Polanski bambino rinchiuso nel ghetto.
articles.body:
Il regista Roman Polanski aveva già raccontato la sua infanzia durante la guerra in un’autobiografia: il muro che nel 1941 vede sorgere intorno al ghetto di Cracovia, i genitori deportati, la madre morta ad Auschwitz, il rifugio presso contadini polacchi. In “Non correte! Andate piano!” torna su quel passato. Per quanto gravi siano i fatti di violenza sessuale per i quali ha riportato condanne o è stato accusato, sarebbe un peccato non leggere il Polanski bambino rinchiuso nel ghetto. Il volume nasce da un’intervista del 2006 per l’Istituto nazionale dell’audiovisivo francese e la fondazione per la memoria della Shoah. Il rigore e l’interrogarsi continuo, accogliendo lacune e incomprensioni dei ricordi, trasformano la testimonianza orale in un ammirevole lavoro di scrittura. Il titolo riprende l’esortazione del lavoratore polacco che lo aiutò a uscire durante il rastrellamento che portò allo sgombero del ghetto, nel marzo 1943. Alle sue parole rispondono due testi del padre Ryszard: una lettera del 1973 sul percorso verso Maut-hausen e un secondo resoconto, datato 1976, sul campo di Płaszów. È una testimonianza agghiacciante e d’immenso coraggio. Il figlio cercava il padre; il padre, scampato più volte alla morte, sopravviveva per ritrovare il figlio. “L’inferno è vuoto, tutti i diavoli sono qui”, cita Polanski dalla Tempesta di Shakespeare, con un’eco del presente. Non è una profezia, ma una constatazione.

Samuel Blumenfeld, Le Monde

“Non correte! Andate piano!”

Alla nuova narrativa argentina, rappresentata da Selva Almada, Federico Falco, Hernán Ronsino e Mauro Libertella, va aggiunto Pablo Katchadjian, che con Grazie dribbla gli avversari. Come il film Gangs of New York e il romanzo Middlesex di Eugenides, il romanzo comincia in un porto. Arrivano schiavi che padroni senza scrupoli selezionano e comprano. Uno di loro, senza nome, è costretto a lavori degradanti. L’umiliazione è tale che le mansioni non vengono descritte: conosciamo solo le reazioni del corpo. Per Walter Benjamin, i reduci tornavano dalla guerra in silenzio perché il trauma li aveva privati dell’esperienza. Così lo schiavo non trova parole per l’orrore: la violenza lo riduce a una cosa. Poi compaiono una bambina selvaggia, fiori dalle radici allucinogene e una serva oppressa. Nascono progetti di rivolta: non un’ideologia, ma il desiderio di un’emancipazione totale. Ucciso il padrone, il protagonista e i compagni partono per liberare altri schiavi, in auto, poi a piedi, incalzati da colonne di fumo. Definirlo solo un romanzo d’avventura sarebbe riduttivo: qui convivono sogno, allucinazione e politica non convenzionale. Non sappiamo dove né quando si svolga. La schiavitù è mutata, non abolita: la società dei consumi maschera lo sfruttamento. Il lavoro interinale non è forse un’evoluzione delle antiche sopraffazioni? Dinamico, divertente e imprevedibile, è all’opposto di quel che ci si aspetta. Katchadjian ha un’immaginazione smisurata.

Joaquín Escobar, Ojo en tinta

Con Le forze, il suo secondo romanzo, la poeta Laura Vazquez propone un libro potente, che rischia di dividere per la forma e la radicalità del discorso. Odissea iniziatica, allucinata e caotica, romanzo-poema destabilizzante, Le forze è un’immersione per tappe nelle profondità dell’animo umano. Attraverso alcuni incontri, esplora contraddizioni, paradossi, alienazioni, fughe in avanti e superficialità, invitandoci a una vasta critica del mondo contemporaneo. La narratrice, una giovane donna che racconta di essere sopravvissuta all’infanzia, si domanda come vivere in un mondo schiacciato dal conformismo, dal denaro, dalla tirannia degli schermi e dalle parole d’ordine del capitalismo, la “grande forza” che nutriamo ogni giorno. Crescendo, ha osservato la sottomissione all’opinione comune, l’adesione passiva agli slogan, la ripetizione dei pregiudizi e il chiacchiericcio vuoto. Il dolore si è accumulato dentro di lei, formando mucchi, piramidi o cristalli. Da tempo porta con sé un’unica, vertiginosa certezza: “Il mondo mente”. Ritrovare la verità sotto le parole, forse perfino farla esistere, è un percorso che dipende dalla poesia, esperienza di osservazione e di linguaggio. Ma “il potere del suono è più grande di quello del senso”.

Christian Desmeules, Le Devoir

Questa raccolta è molto meno spensierata di quanto il titolo possa far pensare: avere un debole per i cowboy può sembrare come una passione per il gelato, ma il bisogno ossessivo di partner incapaci di rispettarti non ha nulla di divertente. Con eroine che si stancano presto degli uomini addomesticati, Pam Houston può sembrare complice del maschio da divano, convinto di perdere il suo fascino primordiale se lava i piatti. Ma le sue protagoniste più originali sono troppo estreme per un maschilismo pigro. Alcol e linguaggio volgare sono giudicati più severamente nelle donne che negli uomini. Ma una così dovrebbe fingersi una pastorella di porcellana? Alcuni racconti, ironici e dolenti, sono poco realistici nella loro fiducia nel cambiamento: sembra basti del buon sesso con un uomo gentile per sistemare il mondo. La natura promette una cura, ma è troppo inospitale per ricavare facili lezioni morali. Altrove colpisce quanto le donne siano disposte a pagare pur di ricevere meno del dovuto. Houston sembra comprendere tutto delle situazioni che descrive, tranne il proprio bisogno di farne parte.

Adam Mars-Jones, The Independent

articles.title: Trump dice ahora que bromeaba al ofrecer su portavocía al presidente de la competición de lucha UFC
articles.summary: El presidente de EE UU ha confirmado que White irá a la Casa Blanca este lunes, aunque “por otra razón”
articles.preview: El presidente de EE UU ha confirmado que White irá a la Casa Blanca este lunes, aunque “por otra razón” El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ha asegurado este domingo que bromeaba cuando publicó que había ofrecido ser portavoz de la Casa Blanca al presidente de la competición de lucha UFC, Dana White. articles.body:
El presidente de EE UU ha confirmado que White irá a la Casa Blanca este lunes, aunque “por otra razón”

El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ha asegurado este domingo que bromeaba cuando publicó que había ofrecido ser portavoz de la Casa Blanca al presidente de la competición de lucha UFC, Dana White. En comentarios cuando regresaba a Washington tras pasar el fin de semana en su residencia de Florida, Mar-a-Lago, el mandatario ha reconocido que “solo fue un chiste”.

En un mensaje en sus redes sociales publicado el sábado, Trump había escrito: “Me complace anunciar que se le ha ofrecido el puesto de jefe de prensa de Estados Unidos al gran Dana White, un violento luchador y combatiente... Dana será un jefe de prensa como ningún otro. ¡Dana, por favor, toma el trabajo!”. El texto estaba acompañado de una imagen de White en el podio del portavoz de la Casa Blanca y fotografías de algunos de los luchadores más famosos de la competición.

Ahora, en declaraciones a los reporteros antes de que su avión despegara hacia la capital estadounidense, el presidente estadounidense ha puntualizado que ese mensaje no iba en serio. “Ya les digo, solo estaba bromeando”, reiteró. Pero también precisó: “A Dana le encanta la idea, y no hay más que un Dana. Ustedes (la prensa) no se atreverían a meterse mucho con él”.

Según Trump, debía haber sido obvio que su mensaje solo pretendía ser un chiste porque en él también instó a White a traer como ayudantes a algunos de los luchadores más famosos de la competición UFC (Ultimate Fighting Championship). “Dije que algunos de ellos vienen de sitios desconocidos. Vienen de muchas áreas, áreas muy peligrosas”.

Pero también ha indicado que “a Dana le gusta la idea, y es un tipo muy capaz”. Trump también ha confirmado que White acudirá este lunes a la Casa Blanca. El dirigente deportivo, al que el comentario del republicano encontró en Londres para asistir a un combate de su competición, había adelantado el sábado por la noche que se vería con el presidente, pero no quiso hacer comentarios sobre la supuesta oferta de trabajo. “Viene de verdad mañana. En realidad, por otra razón... Es un ejemplo de una situación en la que bromeo sobre algo y la gente dice, ‘es una buena idea’”, ha dicho Trump.

“Tenemos una reunión pendiente este lunes y estoy seguro de que hablaremos más que hablar después de ella”, había apuntado White en una rueda de prensa tras el combate en Londres, programada previamente.

La UFC es la competición de artes marciales mixtas de la que Trump ordenó que se celebrara un combate en los jardines de la Casa Blanca por su cumpleaños, en junio pasado.

La Casa Blanca lleva meses sin portavoz, salvo en el breve lapso de cinco días el pasado octubre en que la comentarista conservadora Katie Zacharia ocupó el puesto antes de ser despedida sumariamente. En mayo, la titular del puesto, Karoline Leavitt, tomó una baja por maternidad durante la cual no se nombró a un sustituto. En su lugar, varios miembros del Gabinete se turnaron para ofrecer ruedas de prensa ocasionales en la icónica sala de prensa de la Casa Blanca. Leavitt, de 29 años, llegó a reincorporarse brevemente, pero en agosto anunció su marcha definitiva para dedicar más tiempo a sus dos hijos.

articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.

“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.

Leo stressed the plight of those who, “despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household’s needs”.

He spoke out in defence of the poor and pensioners, insisting that “particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability” – a veiled reference to the government’s controversial cuts to disability assistance.

He also told Milei, known for his foul-mouthed diatribes, that strengthening democracy required a “willingness to listen” and the “careful use of words”.

Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 12-day tour of the continent, just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

The visit is the first by a pontiff to Argentina in nearly four decades, and Leo was met with calls to help mend deep divisions in the country after three years of austerity under Milei.

Argentina is the home country of the late pope, Francis, who Milei famously insulted for his pro-poor teachings.

Leo said he was “retracing” Francis’s steps.

Argentines are hoping the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics will help unite the country, which is bitterly divided between supporters and opponents of Milei.

“Just like the World Cup unites us, hopefully the pope will too,” said Liliana Deblauwe, a 68-year-old retired teacher who waited with hundreds of people to see the pope visit a monument to liberation hero Jose de San Martin.

Hundreds more chanting “Papa Leon” (Spanish for Leo) gathered outside the presidential palace, where he was hosted by Milei.

Brian Inacio Rodriguez, a 26-year-old job seeker, spent five days travelling overland from Ushuaia, at the very tip of South America, to see the pontiff.

He said he hoped he brought “much peace to Argentina”.

Leo arrived in Buenos Aires from Uruguay, where he began his first trip as pope to Latin America, the world’s most Catholic continent which is becoming increasingly secular.

In Uruguay, he condemned drug violence and urged an end to child poverty.

In Buenos Aires, he insisted on the importance of “personal integrity” in public office, stressing that “corruption undermines the confidence of citizens in their institutions.”

The Argentine stage of his visit aims to boost the flagging faith of a country left disappointed by Francis’s failure to visit during his papacy.

It will also act as a litmus test of support for the church. In a recent University of Buenos Aires poll, 57.7% of people identified as Catholic, down from about 90% in the 1960s.

Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses.

The church has said it expects 7 million to attend the various events.

Milei came to office on a promise to revive Argentina’s ailing economy and tame runaway inflation by shrinking the welfare state, targeting public hospitals, universities and pensioners in particular.

The poverty rate has swung wildly since he came to power – increasing to 32.3% in September.

A close ally of US president Donald Trump, with a similar combative style, Milei had a tense relationship with Francis.

On the campaign trail the cost-cutting economist called his countryman an “imbecile” for championing social justice.

Once in office, however, he softened his tone, but he continues to heap insults on the press and opposition.

His relationship with Leo has so far been cordial, but the local Catholic church has heavily criticised him for treating key social services solely as a budgetary constraint.

Milei has also been criticised for restricting several democratic freedoms, including the right to protest. But he maintains a loyal supporter base for drastically reducing inflation.

articles.title: Attacchi hacker, martedì al Viminale un vertice su falle e contromisure
articles.summary: Forse gli allarmi bomba partiti da mail bucate delle scuole. Monitoraggio sulle strutture vulnerabili. Tajani: 'Serve un segnale forte del G7'
articles.preview: Un vertice per monitorare i sistemi informatici ancora vulnerabili, nuovi protocolli per le infrastrutture che necessitano più protezione e valutazione delle piste investigative sui recenti attacchi informatici. Al Viminale martedì prossimo potrebbero essere attuato un giro di vite contro la guerra ibrida: il Comitato nazionale per l'ordine e la sicurezza pubblica, convocato dal ministro dell'Interno, Matteo Piantedosi, riunirà quindi i capi delle forze di polizia e dei servizi di intelligence per approfondire gli aspetti sulla prevenzione ma anche per…
articles.body:
Un vertice per monitorare i sistemi informatici ancora vulnerabili, nuovi protocolli per le infrastrutture che necessitano più protezione e valutazione delle piste investigative sui recenti attacchi informatici. Al Viminale martedì prossimo potrebbero essere attuato un giro di vite contro la guerra ibrida: il Comitato nazionale per l'ordine e la sicurezza pubblica, convocato dal ministro dell'Interno, Matteo Piantedosi, riunirà quindi i capi delle forze di polizia e dei servizi di intelligence per approfondire gli aspetti sulla prevenzione ma anche per capire origine e provenienze dell'offensiva hacker degli ultimi giorni, dai falsi allarmi ai sabotaggi della catena del freddo, fino alle pubblicazioni e la ricerca dei dati sensibili di politici e investigatori da parte dei pirati informatici sul dark web.

Se verrà confermata l'ipotesi che alcuni dei messaggi minatori diretti agli scali aeroportuali italiani siano partiti da mail bucate di scuole, potrebbe essere avviata una riflessione sulla necessità di alzare il livello di difesa informatica degli istituti nel Paese.

Altri messaggi invece erano stati semplicemente anonimizzati con il sistema 'Proton mail'. Insomma, andranno passate al setaccio tutte le falle che hanno permesso ai pirati informatici di agire così facilmente, oltre a uno screening delle infrastrutture ancora troppo esposte, per individuare chi è ancora scoperto e adeguarlo a protocolli più stringenti.

Questo anche alla luce di quegli hackeraggi che alcuni giorni fa avevano colpito persino Montecitorio, dove erano state violate le caselle di posta elettronica di alcuni deputati, compresa quella della premier Giorgia Meloni.

Non a caso il Computer security incident response team Italia (Csirt) ha rilevato che nei primi 9 mesi del 2026 sono stati individuati quasi 45mila asset e servizi a rischio con oltre 3.200 asset potenzialmente compromessi.

Secondo i numeri riportati dall'Acn, nei primi nove mesi del 2026 gli eventi cyber rilevati sono stati 3.271 rispetto ai complessivi 2.729 di tutto il 2025: tra questi, 1.992 classificati come 'incidenti', ovvero eventi con impatto confermato. C'è poi la questione dell'effettiva identità dei cyber criminali e di un eventuale loro coordinamento. Le offensive informatiche in Italia e in tutta Europa si sono diversificate e i riflettori si sono accesi soprattutto sul collettivo filorusso di Noname (alcune azioni sono state effettivamente da loro rivendicate). Ma non c'è alcuna certezza sull'attribuzione di tutti gli attacchi allo stesso gruppo hacker e resta l'ipotesi che possa esserci chi voglia cavalcare la strategia del caos tra le reti informatiche, nascondendosi dietro la sigla dei più noti hacker.

Le indagini sono approfondite ma tutt'altro che terminate; l'Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale ha inviato informative alla Procura nazionale antimafia e antiterrorismo, che sta coordinando gli uffici distrettuali, così come la Polizia postale prosegue nella sua attività investigativa. Una serie di elementi saranno raccolti e confrontati per poi essere portati alla riunione successiva, sempre in settimana, annunciata da Europol, che ha convocato le forze investigative di tutti i Paesi coinvolti negli attacchi di questi giorni.

Aldilà dello specifico focus, alla riunione del Comitato nazionale per l'ordine e la sicurezza pubblica del Viminale - a cui partecipano inoltre i vertici di Polizia, Carabinieri e Guardia di finanza - dovrebbero essere affrontati anche altri temi, come il periodico aggiornamento sull'operazione 'Strade Sicure', che riguarda l'impiego dei militari dell'Esercito dislocati in vari punti sensibili in tutto il Paese, e un punto sulle prossime assunzioni previste nell'ambito della Polizia.

articles.title: Who are the seafarers caught in the US-Israeli war on Iran?
articles.summary: International Maritime Organization records at least 25 deaths since the conflict started on February 28.
articles.preview: International Maritime Organization records at least 25 deaths since the conflict started on February 28. Commercial vessels moving through the Strait of Hormuz and its surrounding waters have come under repeated attack since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran nine months ago. The conflict has transformed one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors into a dangerous passage for crews transporting oil, gas and other goods.
articles.body:
International Maritime Organization records at least 25 deaths since the conflict started on February 28.

Commercial vessels moving through the Strait of Hormuz and its surrounding waters have come under repeated attack since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran nine months ago.

The conflict has transformed one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors into a dangerous passage for crews transporting oil, gas and other goods.

On Sunday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three “rogue oil tankers travelling an unauthorised route” in the strait were subject to “explosions and severe fires”.

The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has recorded the deaths of at least 25 seafarers since the war started on February 28. Many of those killed have been citizens of India, one of the world’s largest suppliers of merchant sailors.

“It is unacceptable that throughout this conflict seafarers have been placed in harm’s way,” the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), a shipping trade association and advocacy group, told Al Jazeera.

“It is incumbent on all parties to take all necessary steps to safeguard the safety of seafarers who are simply going about their job and have found themselves, through no fault of their own, in a highly volatile situation,” an ICS spokesperson added.

The latest incidents have raised questions about the safety of civilian crews, their ability to refuse dangerous assignments and the protections available under international law.

What is happening to ships in the Strait of Hormuz?

The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial passage for international shipping, Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Arabian Sea.

Iran essentially closed the strait after the US-Israeli attacks began, warning that ships trying to sail through the waterway without authorisation could be targeted. Meanwhile, Washington has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Attacks on shipping have involved missiles, projectiles and naval mines that have damaged vessels, set them on fire or sunk them. According to the IMO, at least 129 incidents have been reported.

On Thursday, Iranian forces said five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the strait.

Separately, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker named Velos Sapphire suffered an explosion north of Qatar, killing one crew member.

October was particularly dangerous for commercial shipping with at least 31 vessels hit.

Who are the seafarers being killed or injured?

The victims are largely civilian merchant sailors working on oil tankers, cargo ships and other commercial vessels.

Many come from countries far removed from the conflict, including India, whose nationals have suffered particularly heavy losses, with at least 16 killed.

In June, three Indian sailors were killed in US strikes on commercial vessels near Oman, prompting New Delhi to summon a senior American diplomat.

On Tuesday, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat died after the cargo vessel MSV Al Jusufi was struck off Oman. Thirteen other Indian crew members were rescued.

In October, 12 crew members were injured when the Panamanian-flagged tanker On Peace was struck near Oman. Eleven of those injured were Indian nationals.

People from other countries have also been among the dead. In September, two Filipino crew members were killed when the Saudi tanker Sidr was hit by projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian civilian maritime workers have also suffered casualties.

In May, the head of Iran’s merchant marine union said at least 44 Iranian seafarers had been killed and 29 injured since the start of the war.

What other challenges do seafarers face?

Beyond the threat of death or injury, the war has also taken a toll on sailors’ mental health, according to the ICS spokesperson.

“Shipowners are working hard to ensure that impacted seafarers have access to mental health support services as well as increased access to calls with family and friends,” the spokesperson added.

About 6,000 seafarers remained stranded near the Strait of Hormuz in October, the IMO said in late August.

In March, an arrangement was negotiated between maritime unions and shipping companies through the International Bargaining Forum, under which seafarers could refuse to enter designated danger zones and receive company-funded repatriation and compensation equivalent to two months of basic wages.

At the same time, the International Transport Workers’ Federation said the agreement also provides for increased wages and twice the standard compensation for seafarers who die or suffer a disability.

However, those protections do not necessarily cover every seafarer. And seafarers in the Gulf also face grave mental suffering, maritime charities warned in May, saying many faced loneliness, anxiety and distress.

“As we have throughout the conflict, we strongly urge all ships operating in the region to conduct thorough risk assessments and to maintain vigilance in line with the latest BMP [best management practices] maritime security guidelines,” the ICS spokesperson said.

What does international law say about protecting seafarers during the war?

Under Article 38 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships and aircraft “enjoy the right of transit passage”, a right that no country may suspend.

Article 17 also guarantees foreign vessels the “right of innocent passage” through another country’s territorial waters. Under Article 19, such passage is considered innocent provided it is not “prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal state”.

While the IMO in June sought arrangements to evacuate stranded sailors, efforts to establish safe passage have faced repeated obstacles as attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue unabated.

Academic Abdul Khalique says while international law undoubtedly does apply, “its enforcement is the weak link.”

“The law is clear on the obligations. The gap is political will and practical enforcement,” Khalique, head of the Liverpool John Moores University Maritime Centre, told Al Jazeera.

“For seafarers themselves, legal protections matter most when paired with operational avoidance.”

articles.title: COP31 to open in Turkey, with climate goals under pressure from war and AI
articles.summary: A United Nations Environment Program report said the world is already set to overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above preindustrial times.
articles.preview: ANTALYA, Turkey – Representatives from nearly 200 countries will gather on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast on Monday for two weeks of climate talks, as war-driven energy security fears, surging artificial intelligence power demand and U.S. disengagement put new pressure on the fight against global warming. The U.S. war with Iran has nations scrambling for oil cargoes and firing up coal plants; the rapid rollout of AI is pumping up power demand; and the world’s top historic greenhouse gas emitter is shunning climate cooperation for the second year running.
articles.body:
ANTALYA, Turkey – Representatives from nearly 200 countries will gather on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast on Monday for two weeks of climate talks, as war-driven energy security fears, surging artificial intelligence power demand and U.S. disengagement put new pressure on the fight against global warming.

The U.S. war with Iran has nations scrambling for oil cargoes and firing up coal plants; the rapid rollout of AI is pumping up power demand; and the world’s top historic greenhouse gas emitter is shunning climate cooperation for the second year running.

All that has created a challenging backdrop destined to complicate efforts by COP31 host Turkey to land a strong deal, according to observers.

“It’s hard to be optimistic,” said John Holdren, a professor of environmental policy at Harvard University.

Turkey’s COP31 presidency has centered this year’s U.N.-sponsored summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cookstoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.

But climate advocates have criticized the pledge because it does not require that the additional electricity come from low-carbon sources. This has set up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

A coalition of countries, including South Pacific island nations most vulnerable to sea level rise, are pushing more generally for a clearer global roadmap away from fossil fuels — a perennially controversial topic at climate summits.

Many oil- and gas-producing nations, including Saudi Arabia, argue that fossil fuels can still form a substantial part of the global energy mix in a climate-friendly world, provided they are paired with technologies that reduce or capture emissions.

Pressure is mounting for faster action on climate change.

A report by the United Nations Environment Program published in October said the world is already set to overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above preindustrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit.

2026 also stood out with a series of extreme heat waves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that caused a catastrophic flood that killed more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.

“This year has proven to be one of the years with the highest casualties by the climate-induced disasters,” said Manjeet Dal, an adviser to the Least Developed Country bloc and south Asia director of Climate Analytics.

The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the ensuing sanctions on Moscow’s energy exports. Some say disruptions from the wars have also clarified the benefits of turning to renewables.

The Iran war, now in its ninth month, severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and leading governments to scramble for new supplies.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has encouraged policies maximizing oil, gas, and coal production to address the Mideast disruptions. South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said Holdren of Harvard.

At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China, cheering advocates for ambitious climate action.

“The war has strengthened the case for accelerating the energy transition. The United States is something of an outlier in this regard,” said Andre Correa do Lago, a Brazilian diplomat who presided over last year’s COP.

AI has also added a wrinkle. The technology’s rapid rollout is driving a surge in global power demand, contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions. But its benefits are proving irresistible, even to climate and environment activist groups.

COP31 host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at the conference to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.

Business advocates said they want just one thing from COP31: clarity.

US secretary of state says Iran’s negotiation demands are ‘outrageous and ridiculous, and really not realistic’.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran to safeguard the world from Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

Rubio told reporters in Florida on Sunday that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

Trump addressed “difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary”, Rubio added.

On diplomatic efforts to end the war, Rubio said, “I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough”. He added that although Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.

Rubio comments came after Trump had said that “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President JD Vance recent comments blaming the US-led war on Iran for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in last week’s US midterm elections.

Trump said that although he mostly agreed with Vance, he did not regret the decision to go to war against Iran. It “will go down as one of the best things we ever did”, he said, adding that if Tehran were to have a nuclear weapon, “they would blow up the world”.

Trump also told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday that as long as Washington sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a “strong agreement”, it is “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” for the US to resume strikes.

For Iran’s part, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that it was “time for the White House to make its own” decision on the war.

“American voters have made their choice,” Araghchi wrote on X, referring to the midterm election results.

He added that Tehran’s “2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results”.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Iran has offered to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within two days if the United States meets its conditions.

Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.

Tehran is reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with Washington, according to the Associated Press news agency.

In recent days, Rubio has also denied “unfounded” speculation that he was quitting as the top US diplomat to run for higher office in 2028.

Even after the start of Syria’s civil war in 2011, beekeeper Muhammad Salih regularly traveled along the country’s northern border with Turkey in search of the best spots to produce the honey that sustained his family. But while Salih has left sectarian violence behind, he hasn’t been able to escape extreme weather. Drought has cut his honey production in half over the past five years. This year, the rains returned but brought intense flooding and hail that destroyed the flowers his business depends on.

Chants of "Free Palestine" and "Shame on you" echoed through the crowds, while marchers demanded action from The Hague. Organisers called for tougher trade sanctions against Israel, a halt to arms sales and official recognition of Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide. The protest comes amid continuing tensions between the Netherlands and Israel over the humanitarian situation in Gaza. Israel strongly rejects accusations of genocide, maintaining that its military campaign followed the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, which killed around 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who joined an earlier Red Line demonstration but did not attend Sunday's march, defended his government's approach, saying it was increasing diplomatic pressure on Israel while also pressing Hamas to respect security commitments.

articles.title: Ucraina: Europei e Francia al trilaterale di Abu Dhabi, ma i Volenterosi si esercitano
articles.summary: Da lunedì in Polonia manovre militari per il dopo guerra in Ucraina. 'Raid su soccorsi'
articles.preview: Alla vigilia dell'incontro tecnico ad Abu Dhabi, il trilaterale tra Russia, Ucraina e Usa si trasforma in un multilaterale allargandosi al vecchio continente, che tuttavia non rinuncia a lanciare quasi contemporaneamente le prime esercitazioni dei Volenterosi pro Kiev, in Polonia. È stato il ministro degli Esteri francese Jean-Noël Barrot a rompere il velo di riservatezza sul cambio di format: "Gli europei saranno adeguatamente rappresentati e la Francia sarà ad Abu Dhabi per partecipare a queste discussioni", ha dichiarato.
articles.body:
Alla vigilia dell'incontro tecnico ad Abu Dhabi, il trilaterale tra Russia, Ucraina e Usa si trasforma in un multilaterale allargandosi al vecchio continente, che tuttavia non rinuncia a lanciare quasi contemporaneamente le prime esercitazioni dei Volenterosi pro Kiev, in Polonia.

È stato il ministro degli Esteri francese Jean-Noël Barrot a rompere il velo di riservatezza sul cambio di format: "Gli europei saranno adeguatamente rappresentati e la Francia sarà ad Abu Dhabi per partecipare a queste discussioni", ha dichiarato. "Non posso ancora dirvi chi rappresenterà la Francia in quell' occasione, ma la Francia ci sarà", ha proseguito.

"Ci sono state discussioni, a volte senza gli europei, a volte con loro. Questa volta vi parteciperanno. La Francia sarà presente e farà sentire la voce dell'Europa", ha assicurato il titolare del Quai d' Orsay, che nelle grandi crisi internazionali tende a promuovere il formato E3 (Francia, Germania, Gb) in coordinamento con la responsabile della diplomazia europea Kaja Kallas.

L'annuncio arriva pochi giorni dopo che la premier Giorgia Meloni ha denunciato in una lettera al presidente del Consiglio Ue Antonio Costa l'approccio "in ordine sparso" dei Paesi europei nei negoziati sull'Ucraina, rilanciando la "necessità ormai improcrastinabile" per la Ue "di parlare con una sola voce" su questo conflitto. Nella lettera Meloni aveva elencato i troppi formati degli ultimi tempi e aveva detto di aver saputo di "una non meglio precisata presenza europea ai colloqui previsti ad Abu Dhabi tra ucraini e russi con la mediazione americana".

Presenza che rimane imprecisata anche dopo l'uscita di Barrot. Pure Jared Kushner, inviato di Trump nonché suo genero, aveva ventilato giovedì scorso un allargamento del formato agli europei, ma subordinato ad eventuali passi avanti nei negoziati: gli Stati Uniti, aveva detto, "si consulteranno strettamente con i loro partner europei" a margine dei colloqui di Abu Dhabi e "qualora si registrassero dei progressi, l'obiettivo sarà quello di evolvere verso un formato multilaterale più ampio, con la loro partecipazione diretta".

I colloqui negli Emirati Arabi dovrebbero consentire di delineare una possibile via d'uscita dal conflitto, con un accordo che, secondo Donald Trump, "potrebbe coinvolgere l'intera Europa". Gli europei e Kiev hanno però messo in guardia contro qualsiasi ipotesi di un'"architettura di sicurezza" che venisse delineata alle loro spalle. Kushner, secondo il Washington Post, punterebbe a un modello tipo il Consiglio Nato-Russia, istituito dopo la Guerra Fredda ma sospeso nel 2014, in seguito all'annessione della Crimea.

Nel frattempo, lunedì partono le prime esercitazioni militari della Forza multinazionale per l'Ucraina (Mnf-u), il "braccio militare" dei Volenterosi in vista del dopoguerra: principalmente in Polonia, ma, come spiegato dal generale di Corpo d'Armata britannico Bateman, responsabile dell' addestramento 'Koalicja', anche in Turchia e Francia. In campo, sino al 22 novembre, 2.800 soldati, di cui circa 1.100 francesi, 300 britannici e gli altri appartenenti agli eserciti di Belgio, Estonia, Germania, Lituania, Paesi Bassi, Polonia, Spagna, Svezia e Turchia.

E mentre i dem vittoriosi a Midterm stanno cercando di mettere insieme un nuovo pacchetto di aiuti da 15 miliardi per Kiev, Mosca continua ad attaccare l'Ucraina: anche a Komyshuvakha, "dove da sette giorni sono in corso operazioni di soccorso dopo un bombardamento che ha ucciso 55 persone", ha denunciato Zelensky parlando di "un cinismo e una crudeltà assoluti". L'offensiva russa però paga un prezzo umano altissimo sul fronte terrestre: secondo i dati rubati all'agenzia di statistica russa Rosstat dal gruppo bielorusso filo-opposizione Cyber Partisans e dagli hacker ucraini Silent Crow, fra il febbraio 2022 e la fine di agosto 2026 sono stati registrati 392.700 certificati di morte legati esplicitamente alla guerra in Ucraina.
